reviewMethod: Inspected all 48 frames through four 12-frame contact sheets, then inspected the three full-resolution key stills and full-resolution frames 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30 and 32 around the derived detachment event.

questions.question: Does the cause frame show a recognizable basketball, three readable bottles and an attached cap before impact?
questions.observation: The wide cause shot clearly establishes one worn basketball, three differently filled and labeled bottles, the court, scale cues and attached caps.

questions.question: Is the basketball-to-bottle contact continuous without an obvious gap or penetration?
questions.observation: The fixed-camera sequence closes continuously into contact; silhouette overlap reads as foreground occlusion during impact rather than a teleport or visible gap.

questions.question: Does the cap remain visibly attached before the measured primary contact?
questions.observation: All bottle tops read as capped before frame 16 and no secondary object appears early.

questions.question: Does cap separation begin only after the collision and remain causally readable?
questions.observation: Machine evidence derives separation at frame 24, but the fixed contact camera places the cap behind the ball and bottle cluster, so the separation is not visually readable.

questions.question: Does the cap follow one continuous trajectory without teleporting or a hand-authored-looking jump?
questions.observation: The cap trajectory is solver-continuous in measurements but is occluded for the decisive frames; visual continuity cannot be verified from the rendered clip.

questions.question: Does the detached object still read at bottle-cap scale with recognizable cap material and shape?
questions.observation: The detached cap never becomes a clearly identifiable silver crimped cap in the reviewed frames or effect still.

questions.question: Do at least two bottles respond continuously while their final poses remain visibly unstaged?
questions.observation: All three bottles respond through distinct tilts and rolls; two fall in different directions and one remains upright without symmetry or posed final alignment.

questions.question: Does the secondary response add physical richness without becoming an explosive or chaotic effect?
questions.observation: The primary collision is controlled, but the secondary response adds almost no perceptible richness because it is hidden.

questions.question: Does the derived effect shot include the response bottles and detached cap with useful occupancy?
questions.observation: The settled effect shot frames the bottles well, but the detached cap is not identifiable or given useful screen separation.

questions.question: Do the court lighting, enclosure, material readability and shot progression still feel filmic without fake debris, particles or camera shake?
questions.observation: Warm court light, cool fill, floor reflections and stable framing remain coherent and no decorative effect substitutes for physics.

failureReason: The physical event passes every machine check, but the secondary event is camera-occluded and therefore not communicable as film.
requiredCorrection: Derive the contact and effect camera directions from secondary-body screen-space readability, testing bounded generic azimuth candidates and choosing the one with the greatest cap-to-primary projected separation. Do not move any physical object or change simulation.
